newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Perry heads to Kuwait to tighten noose on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Perry heads to Kuwait to tighten noose on Iraq.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry tries to tighten a military noose around President Saddam Hussein on Sunday when he discusses with ally Kuwait ways of handling fresh confrontation with the Iraqi leader.

Kuwait, grateful to Washington for leading its 1991 Gulf War liberation from seven months of Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to give the United States full backing in its latest standoff with Saddam.

Perry is due to arrive in Kuwait on a regional tour to talk to senior Gulf Arab officials about possible "future measures" against Iraq, Kuwaiti Information Minister Sheikh Saud al-Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah said on Saturday.

He did not spell out the measures. But a Western military analyst in Kuwait said Washington was keen to stress to its regional allies, some reluctant to get directly involved in the military buildup, the need to deal firmly with Saddam.
"The Americans want a free hand (in dealing with Iraq), there is no doubt about that," said the analyst. The United States "wants to make sure that no one messes with Uncle Sam in the Gulf."
Kuwait's government said in a statement to parliament: "This (Iraqi) regime does not understand anything but force and this regime will always create tension in the region."

While most regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington is sending more warships to the region and 5,000 troops to Kuwait. Eight Stealth bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday as part of preparations for a possible military strike against Iraq.

The deployment was widely welcomed in Kuwait where many citizens informally celebrate former U.S. president George Bush's birthday and name their sons after the man who led the Gulf War coalition. Even a new luxury residential building overlooking the Gulf has been named after him.
President Bill Clinton said in a weekly radio address he had placed a "strategic strait-jacket" on Saddam by sending enough military force to the Gulf to keep him in check.
Kuwait, a small oil-exporting state of two million people, is the only regional country that has allowed U.S. warplanes and troops to deploy on its territory during the latest flare-up.
Kuwait defended the large U.S. deployment on its territory, saying it was an act of sovereignty within the terms of defence pacts with Gulf War coalition states.
But at a meeting in Cairo, Arab states, including U.S. Gulf Arab allies, condemned American cruise missile attacks on Iraq this month, saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.

Analysts say Arab states are mainly concerned that a weakened Baghdad or Saddam's downfall could result in Iraq's disintegration into three states -- a Kurdish north, a Moslem Shi'ite Moslem south and an Arab country in central Iraq.
"It is not out of love for Saddam (they take this stand), it is fear of making the problem even worse for everybody," including the West, one analyst said.

Kuwait's Sheikh Saud stressed he was not advocating Saddam's downfall but said: "The crisis will never be over until Saddam Hussein goes. This cat-and-mouse game has to stop...Some kind of measures will have to be taken to put an end to this."
Kuwaiti and Western officials say Iraq must do more to avert further U.S. strikes, including making all air defences in an expanded southern no-fly zone non-operational.
Following the missile strikes on September 3 and 4, U.S. warplanes started enforcing a wider no-fly zone in southern Iraq, extending it to the outskirts of Baghdad.
